name: Udd distal myopathy / tibial muscular dystrophy (titin)

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant late-onset distal myopathy caused by variants in the C-terminal (M-line) region of the titin gene (TTN), with a well-described Finnish founder mutation
Onset is usually after the age of 35-40 years, with slowly progressive weakness of the anterior lower-leg muscles, particularly the tibialis anterior, causing foot drop
Weakness and atrophy are often relatively selective for the tibialis anterior on imaging, with the deep posterior and other compartments spared until later

Heterozygotes typically have a mild distal phenotype and retain ambulation, whereas homozygous or compound heterozygous TTN variants cause a severe limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD R10, formerly LGMD2J)
Creatine kinase is normal or mildly elevated and electromyography confirms a myopathic process
Muscle biopsy shows dystrophic or myopathic changes, often with rimmed vacuoles
Muscle MRI demonstrating selective anterior tibial involvement is a useful diagnostic pointer
Diagnosis rests on the anterior-compartment distal weakness pattern together with TTN genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Udd myopathy results from dominant variants affecting the C-terminal M-line region of titin, the giant sarcomeric protein that spans from the Z-disc to the M-line and provides passive elasticity and a scaffold for sarcomere assembly and signalling. Mutations disrupt the interaction of titin with M-line binding partners such as calpain-3, impairing sarcomeric integrity and maintenance. The anterior lower-leg muscles are affected earliest, producing distal weakness and foot drop, while a double dose of TTN variants causes more widespread muscle breakdown and a severe limb-girdle phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Laing distal myopathy and other anterior-compartment distal myopathies
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and peroneal neuropathy causing foot drop
L5 radiculopathy or common peroneal nerve palsy
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to distinguish myopathy from neuropathy
Muscle MRI showing selective tibialis anterior involvement
Muscle biopsy for dystrophic changes and rimmed vacuoles
Targeted TTN M-line sequencing or a comprehensive distal myopathy/LGMD panel
Family evaluation given dominant inheritance and the severe recessive limb-girdle phenotype
redFlags: Severe early-onset generalised weakness suggesting a homozygous limb-girdle titinopathy
Cardiac symptoms, since some TTN variants are associated with cardiomyopathy
Respiratory muscle weakness with declining vital capacity
Rapid progression atypical for the classic heterozygous phenotype
reference.prognosis: The heterozygous tibial muscular dystrophy phenotype progresses slowly, and most patients retain independent walking with a normal lifespan; homozygous or compound heterozygous disease produces a much more severe, disabling limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.
pitfalls: Mistaking the foot drop for a peroneal nerve palsy or radiculopathy
Failing to consider a severe recessive titinopathy in relatives when counselling families
Assuming normal creatine kinase excludes myopathy
Overlooking possible cardiac involvement associated with certain titin variants
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy exists, so care centres on physiotherapy and a stretching programme to preserve ankle range and function against the tibialis anterior weakness
Ankle-foot orthoses to correct foot drop and improve gait stability and safety
Occupational therapy and mobility aids to maintain independence as distal weakness progresses
Respiratory and cardiac assessment, particularly in the severe homozygous or compound heterozygous limb-girdle phenotype where more widespread muscle involvement occurs
Multidisciplinary follow-up through a neuromuscular clinic with periodic reassessment of functional status
Genetic counselling and family evaluation given autosomal dominant inheritance and the severe recessive limb-girdle phenotype in offspring of two carriers
